Messages.Author: Cecil
Messages.Body:
I've been working with both a Ravnos and a Nos wall deck recently, and I
was wondering if I could get some help with strategy. There is one main
problem that I am having… Without advanced Auspex, my prey normally
resorts to doing things I can't block. Bleeds, D-actions to other
Meth's. My chances to disable my prey is low, what can I do to stop
that? Pack rush and bleed mod's come to mind.

I also have 2 strategy questions about walls:
1. I am not sure whether to stay untapped or to use untaps. Which is
more effective? Both of these decks use lots of permanent intercept
(Raptors for Nos, Masters + Ravens for Ravnos) and some surprise
intercept (Nos have cats guidance and some auspex for C. Robin, Draba
and Ignis Fatuus for Ravnos). Does the threat of remaining untapped work
better, or is surprise a better element to use in your favor?
2. Is the purpose of a wall deck to be the last deck standing? That is
normally what mine does, and the best I can do is tie.

Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
In message
<Pine.GSO.4.21.030612...@petsparc.duhs.duke.edu>,
David Cherryholmes <david.che...@duke.edu> mumbled something
about:



A corollary to this: the only way a wall deck can lose the GW is to let
its prey get any VP, or to let the table time out in some fashion.

Reread that carefully. I know it'll surprise some people.

A wall deck has complete control over the GW. The only way it can FAIL
to gain the win is:

- Allow its prey to get 3VP, eliminating anyone else from contention for
the Game Win.
- Allow its prey to get 2VP and someone else to get 1VP, guaranteeing
that the best the wall deck can do is tie or allow another player to get
a GW.
- Allow its prey to get 1VP and someone else to get 2VP,... see above.
- Let the table time out, guaranteeing that nobody gets a GW.

None of these are an acceptable option when playing a wall deck.
Therefore, a wall deck should have two primary focii: first, preventing
its prey from EVER gaining a VP by any means necessary, and second,
ensuring that the table does not time out under any circumstances.

The first criteria mandates the use of Eagle's Sight, which mandates
superior Auspex. No other means is sufficient. Even Eagle's Sight may
not be enough against certain decks of your prey, but it will do for
most.

In addition, the first criteria also mandates that as few as possible of
your prey's actions be successful. No action which causes damage to
your grandprey, or gains your prey pool in some fashion, should be
allowed to complete if at all possible. Judgement is required here --
if you're going to get killed blocking a bleed of 1, perhaps you should
let it by. But your minions' survival is secondary to the Game Win;
since you know you cannot win by inaction, you should be as
antimaterialistic as necessary to stop your prey from gaining VP.
Occasionally this will mean exploding one of your own minions, but it
may be necessary.

The second criteria can only be satisfied by cards such as the
much-reviled Anarch Revolt and Smiling Jack. HOWEVER! This does not
mean you should pitch Anarchs out of your hand like they're going out of
style (Peter Bakija, I see you lurking in the back). Instead, keep one
or two Anarchs in play at all times. Do not block attempts to remove
them (unless of course your prey tries) -- they've already hurt the most
important person, your prey. Combined with the heavy chain you're tying
around your prey's ankles, your prey should be almost completely unable
to do anything other than be pitifully ousted by the Anarchs -- since of
course your own blood gain via Blood Dolls and just
not-taking-pool-damage should be more than sufficient to outlast him.

Once your prey is dead, let's pause for a moment and review our
criteria. First, our prey has gotten no VPs, and we have 1. The table
is definitely not going to time out, because the Anarchs and possibly
Jack are being a dead weight on even the strongest bloat decks. What
could be happening on the rest of the table? Only a few things:

- It is very likely that our grandprey, having no pressure at all on him
all game, has ousted our grandpredator and predator, gaining 2VP.
However, he still has to oust us to ensure the table win, and we have
the upper hand on him since our deck, like all wall decks, becomes a
monster in a 1-on-1 situation. We like this situation, especially with
Anarchs on the table forcing their hand and denying them the
"bloat-and-get-ten-minions" approach. The only problem is going to be
that we MUST obtain the Edge as soon as possible to deny pool gain, and
our deck does not have a lot of room for stealth. A few Night Moves
might be an excellent choice.

- Our grandprey is pathetic, and our grandpredator has ousted our
predator, gaining 1VP. (or our grandprey has ousted our grandpredator
but has not yet finished the job on our predator, either way.) While
our deck is strong in a three-player environment, the conditions are not
yet ideal for us to be able to force the situation and win. We would
like it to be 1-on-1. Conveniently, we are able to do this by changing
strategy -- completely ignore our prey, and kill our predator
ruthlessly. Once our predator is ousted, the score will be 1-1-1, and
we are in the "duel" situation that we wanted in the first place. We
should be able to handily win from here.

- The entire table is flailing helplessly under the weight of the
Anarchs. Sit back, defend, gain pool, and watch to see which of the
above two situations it becomes. With the Anarchs out, it shouldn't
take long for SOMEONE to fall into the well.

Are we likely to be the table target? Well... the Anarchs will not make
you popular, but once it's clear that you're not going to go nuts with
them or prevent them from being removed, people will calm down somewhat.
Your prey is going to be pretty pissy about it (as well he should be;
he's the one taking it in the ass), but your grandprey is going to
completely be your friend. Since your grandprey has no pressure, he is
very likely to become the table target himself -- he'll have a lot more
forward motion than you do, and that draws attention whether or not
people realize it.

By the time it's a three player game, everyone is a target anyway. Your
task is to avoid being targeted during the 4-player or 5-player phases;
from that point forward you'll be in a lot better shape.

I repeat: Eagle's Sight is mandatory.

Many decks take nothing but (D) actions. Stealth bleed, for example.
Stealth bleed is your primary danger, in fact -- it will take nothing
but (D) actions, and if you miss catching them once it may oust its prey
and THEN where will you be?

Skilled players, when they realize that you're playing heavy intercept,
immediately reduce their stealth as low as possible and take nothing but
(D) actions, in an attempt to jam you on intercept and catch you without
Eagle's Sight. Many undirected actions are no longer necessary when you
have a predator who is putting little direct pressure on you -- the
Govern at superior that you were counting as pool gain, for example,
suddenly turns into a bleed.

The only way you luck out and DON'T need Eagle's Sight is if you happen
to be the predator of a vote deck. And even those often include a good
hunk of bleed in them.

you've caught your prey.

able to catch your prey, your game is pretty much over anyway.

If the ousting strategy is Anarch Revolt and/or Smiling Jack, why
would the rest of the table be oblivious to this and not try to get
rid of them? And if you're not stopping attempts to get rid of them,
how are you ousting people at all?

I think you're underestimating the table reaction to seeing an
Anarch Revolt and/or Smiling Jack on the table. Those cards aren't
thrown in casually. They're very obviously part of the offensive
plan of a...oh, wait a minnit, you should be using Antediluvian
Awakening in there, too...at any rate, they're very obviously part
of the offensive plan of the deck that plays them. If you're looking
to stop or slow down that deck, target the Anarch Revolts and the
Smiling Jacks.

So, now that we're assuming that the table recognizes the Anarch
Revolt/Smiling Jack threat for what it is - the key to your offensive
strategy - how do you go about ousting someone once those offensive
measures have been eliminated?

On top of that, it's certainly fair for other deck strategies to ask
the question "How do I break through the wall?"

One way you can do it is to either overload its ability to intercept
or overload its ability to fight. A focussed stealth-bleeder typically
makes a mockery of an intercept deck. A focussed combat deck can
overload an intercept-combat deck by not having as many of those pesky
intercept cards diluting the deck.

Something you can do cross-table is mess with the wall deck's
infrastructure. They're typically getting out The Rack, a Hunting
Ground, Powerbase: Montreal, and so on. Taking actions to steal the
Rack or Montreal really annoys an wall deck, as cross-table actions
are a strain on the defense/untap of a wall deck. Similarly, rescuing
the wall deck's prey's minions cross table really drives them nuts, as
it removes opportunities to catch the prey taking actions, and helps
keep the prey moving forward.

These (and other) counter-wall strategies then get the wall deck
thinking about what to do design-wise to counter them...Hybrids of
intercept-combat and bruise-bleed, adding stealth back into the
Tzimisce decks, Millicent Smith to help protect Smiling Jack, etc.

minimize need to control. When all you have to control is your prey and
your predator, you're in good shape.

harass it" action. Club Zombie as well, and let's not forget the good
old Hungry Coyote for personal pool gain. While it's possible to steal
these, obviously, it's not as easy since your deck has to have the card
in hand; I feel a lot safer about blocking a single Arson action, for
example.

Grim. Once you start second-guessing yourself you back even further
into the hole, though. A certain amount of toolbox is necessary, but...

Messages.Body:
Howdy,

> Is there a bigger threat to an intercept-combat deck than cross-table
> rescuing?

Sitting next to _another_ intercept combat deck? If it's your prey,
all of your untap and intercept are dead cards, unless your predator
is feeling suicidal. If it's your predator your chances of winning
the one-on-one are kind of iffy. As a bonus, contesting Mr. Winky,
KRCG, etc. is like your own personal Anarch.

As noted by others, sitting next to rush combat is not a lot of fun
either, as it typically takes fewer cards to put the 'rush' in rush
combat than it takes to put the 'intercept' in intercept combat, and
so there's more room for the 'combat' part. It usually comes down to
the particular rock-paper-scissors of the combat types, though, in
both cases, and even in some bruise/bleed cases.

Finally, sitting next to weenies can make it tricky for any kind of
combat - there's just so many minions to catch or block, though they
do generally make a satisfying crunchy noise when apprehended.
Intercept has the advantage here, at least if it's packing Atonement,
Eternal Vigilance, Tension, etc. Fame is good for rush, though watch
for auto-diablerie. Still, even if you do manage to oust the weenie
player, you may go through too much deck doing it.

Thoughts from the Master upon these situations?

Thanks,
Alex

I was going with the presumption that the intercept decks are both

Of course it's not a zero-sum game; it's entirely possible for you
both to just wreck each other, leaving some other player to clean up.
In fact, that's usually the case when I try intercept - I wound
myself, my predator, and (hopefully) my prey, and then my
grandpredator sweeps up. Very reminiscent of poorly played rush, I
know. But it is at least indicative that I'm trying to go forward.
(And that I keep trying to win with !Ventrue...)

I'm convinced intercept is at least as hard to learn as rush, if not
more difficult, as the balance (forward vs. backward) is much more
delicate and less predictable. (The rush maxim: Burned minions take
no actions!) I suppose people will disagree with me there, but I
think that most people who find intercept 'easy' are happy with 2 VP,
which _is_ much easier than winning the table in the manner which
Derek has expounded upon so elegantly.

Hope that helps,
Alex

it does.

Tacking on enough bleed to provide significant offense sort of obviates
the definition of 'wall deck'. Token bleed is usually the order of the
day, but this is typically counterproductive for the wall deck as it
permits its prey to play whatever its bleed defense cards are.

carefully before flying off the handle.
